slides.say: Given: x plus the absolute value of x is smaller than twelve. What is the most precise domain for x?
So first, what does most precise mean? The domain has to hold exactly the numbers that work, no more and no less. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, two cases, and plugging in the answers.

slides: [short pause] Our first method, two cases. The bars act differently on each side of zero, so that's where we split.

slides.say: Within this first case, x is restricted to the zero-or-positive side. Let's find which values on that side satisfy the inequality. Case one, x is zero or positive. Then the bars do nothing, the absolute value of x is just x. So x plus x is smaller than twelve. Two x is smaller than twelve, and twelve divided by two is six, so x is smaller than six.

Now case two, and careful here, because this is the case people lose. x is negative. Then the bars turn x into its opposite, so the absolute value of x is minus x. And x plus minus x? Opposites attract, so they cancel out to zero.
Let's see it in numbers. Minus four plus four is zero. Minus nine plus nine is zero. Always zero.
And is zero smaller than twelve? Yes, every time. So every negative number works.

We need the combined set of values that work in either case, including zero, which works in the first case. Put the two cases together. Every negative number, and the positives below six. That's every number below six. On the number line, one ray going left from six, an open circle at six, and no stop at minus six.
So x smaller than six, choice number three is our answer.

[pause] Our second method, plugging in the answers. One number that breaks a choice crosses it out. Let's try zero first. Why zero? Because the choices disagree about zero, two of them include it and two leave it out. Zero plus zero is zero, smaller than twelve, so zero works.
But choice number two says x is smaller than zero, and choice number four says x is bigger than zero. Both leave zero out. So one number kills two choices.

The remaining choices agree about the upper boundary but disagree about the lower boundary. Let's test a value that only one of them includes. Choice numbers one and three both stop at six on top. The difference is the bottom, minus six, or no limit at all. So I test a number below minus six, minus eight.
Minus eight plus its absolute value, eight, is zero. Zero is smaller than twelve, so it works. So x can go below minus six, and choice number one misses those numbers. Choice number three.
